body.heading: The power of halving
paragraphs: In Twenty Questions, one player thinks of a person, place or thing, and the others may ask twenty questions that can only be answered yes or no. It sounds hopeless — the world is a big place. But a yes-or-no answer carries exactly one bit of information, and bits add up fast.

Every perfect question cuts the possibilities in half. After one question, half the world is gone. After ten questions, you have narrowed things by a factor of about a thousand. After twenty, you have sorted through 2 to the power 20 — 1,048,576 possibilities. A million things, found with twenty careful questions.

body.heading: Ask big questions first
paragraphs: The art is in asking questions that split the remaining possibilities near the middle. 'Is it alive?' halves the world. 'Is it bigger than a house?' is useful. 'Is it a specific celebrity I happen to be thinking of?' wastes a question on a one-in-a-million guess.

Work from the general to the particular: alive or not, then animal or plant or person, then wild or tame, then size, then habitat — and save the naming guess for the very end, when the space is small enough to see across.

body.heading: Play it this week
paragraphs: Play a round tonight with one rule upgrade: after each answer, the guessers must say out loud roughly how many possibilities they think remain. It turns a party game into a visible demonstration of halving — the numbers collapse faster than anyone expects.
Computers search the same way, in a method called binary search: guess the middle, halve, repeat. You have been doing it since childhood, one yes at a time.

takeaway: Every yes-or-no answer can halve the search space — twenty good questions can find one thing in a million.
